headline: Connecticut housing costs account for 21% of poverty, Pew analysis finds
dek: The analysis says above-average rents are tied to 26% of child poverty in the state, putting housing supply and zoning at the center of the affordability debate.
body: Above-average housing costs account for 21% of poverty in Connecticut and 26% of child poverty, according to a new analysis by [The Pew Charitable Trusts](https://www.pew.org/en/research-and-analysis/articles/2026/09/29/the-housing-shortage-is-a-major-driver-of-poverty). The findings put a familiar Connecticut complaint—high rent and too few available homes—into a broader measure of household hardship: housing costs are not only squeezing budgets, but also pushing some families below a poverty threshold that adjusts for local expenses.

The analysis examines 2023 housing costs and uses the U.S. Census Bureau’s Supplemental Poverty Measure, or SPM. Unlike the official poverty measure, the SPM accounts for government benefits, taxes and geographic differences in expenses, including housing. Pew says Connecticut was among 10 states where above-average housing costs made up the largest shares of poverty, and Connecticut tied for seventh in the study. That means the headline percentages are estimates from a model, not a count of residents who listed rent as the reason they became poor.

The distinction matters for how the results should be read. Pew researchers looked at what would happen if rents fell relative to the national average while other household costs stayed the same. In that hypothetical, a 20% decline in inflation-adjusted rents would lower the average poverty threshold for Connecticut families with children by $3,905, according to the report. The exercise does not predict that rents will fall or promise that every family would see the same savings; it shows how strongly housing costs affect the income a household needs to remain above the SPM line.

Connecticut Public, which reported on the analysis Monday, quoted Pew housing-policy project director Alex Horowitz saying the state is in a “long-term landlords market,” with tenants competing for scarce homes. Horowitz attributed that pressure to a shortage of housing and told the public broadcaster that the effect can blunt help from programs such as SNAP, Housing Choice Vouchers and the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit. When rent rises faster than a household’s resources, assistance can cover less of the family’s actual needs even if the benefit itself has not changed.

The report’s policy argument is that reducing poverty requires attention to costs as well as income. Pew points to zoning, building-code and permitting rules that can make it harder or more expensive to add homes. The analysis also cites examples in Austin and Minneapolis where inflation-adjusted rents fell by about 20% after changes intended to allow more housing. Those examples do not establish that Connecticut would see the same result, but they provide the comparison behind Pew’s estimate that lower rents could reduce poverty by 18% to 26% and child poverty by 21% to 38% in the high-cost states it studied.

Horowitz told Connecticut Public that lawmakers could ease the pressure by making it possible to build smaller apartment buildings, reducing some lot-size requirements and allowing more townhomes, condominiums and apartments through zoning changes. He also said Connecticut ranked 49th nationally in housing production per person from 2017 through 2023. That figure is a production comparison cited by the report’s local coverage, not a claim that every municipality has the same shortage or that new construction alone would immediately make every neighborhood affordable.

The analysis does not settle several questions that will shape the state’s response. It does not identify which Connecticut cities or towns account for the largest share of the housing-related poverty estimate, nor does it say how many homes would need to be built to produce a 20% statewide rent decline. It also does not remove the need for targeted aid: Pew says the lowest-income households would still need vouchers and other subsidies even if rents fell. The study therefore presents housing production and direct assistance as complementary tools rather than substitutes.

For Connecticut families, the near-term effect is mainly political and practical. The findings give state and local officials a way to connect housing approvals, zoning rules and rental supply to poverty policy, while the SPM framework offers a more realistic picture of costs than an income-only measure. The next test will be whether Connecticut can add homes quickly enough, in places where people need them, without assuming that a statewide percentage automatically describes every renter’s experience.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Connecticut housing costs drive poverty, Pew analysis finds
seoDescription: A Pew analysis says above-average housing costs account for 21% of poverty and 26% of child poverty in Connecticut.
